items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (Electron cloud): A student draws the electron in a hydrogen atom as a dot moving on a circular track. Explain what an electron-cloud diagram shows instead, and what the darker regions mean.

answer.html: The electron cloud shows where the electron is likely to be found. The electron has no fixed circular track; the darker, denser regions are places where the probability of finding the electron is higher, and lighter regions are less likely.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 28 question: An atom has two levels that differ by 1.96 eV. A photon of 1.96 eV stimulates the atom to emit a second photon. Find the wavelength of each of the two photons.

body.html: In stimulated emission the new photon has the same energy as the stimulating photon, so both have 𝜆= ℎ𝑐/ 𝐸.

answer.html: Both photons have a wavelength of 633 nm (red), since both carry the energy 1.96 eV.

check.html: 1.96 eV is within the visible range of 1.8 to 3.1 eV, and red light is expected at the low-energy end.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (Stimulated emission): In a ruby laser, a 694 nm photon stimulates an excited atom to emit a second photon. Compare the two photons, and find the energy of each.

body.html: Energy of each photon: 𝐸= 1240 / 694 = 1.79 eV.

answer.html: The two photons have the same energy (1.79 eV), frequency and wavelength (694 nm), they travel in the same direction and they are in phase (coherent).

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (Surveying): Which characteristics of laser light make it suited to aligning a long tunnel under construction?

answer.html: A laser beam is narrow and directional (it barely spreads), intense, and has one wavelength, so it makes a straight, bright reference line over a long distance that workers and sensors can follow accurately.

items.title: Lesson 4, Investigate (Applying Practices, communicate technology information): Choose a technology that uses light and quantum physics, and explain how it works to the class.

body.html: Sample: a barcode scanner uses a red laser beam swept across the code; the dark bars reflect less light than the white spaces, and a photocell converts the reflected photons to an electric signal (the photoelectric effect). An LED works when electrons drop between energy levels in a semiconductor and emit photons whose energy equals the gap.

answer.html: Open-ended; the sample device descriptions above show the expected level of detail.

items.title: 47: A student claims the Bohr model should be able to predict the spectrum of helium and should be correct that electrons move on circular orbits. Evaluate the claim.

answer.html: The claim is wrong. The Bohr model works only for hydrogen-like atoms with one electron, and cannot predict the spectrum of helium (two electrons) or other atoms. The quantum model replaces fixed circular orbits with probability clouds, because an electron's exact position and path cannot be known.

items.title: 48: Could 450 nm blue light pump a 650 nm red laser? Could 850 nm infrared light pump a 590 nm yellow laser?

body.html: Pumping needs photons with energy at least as large as the excitation energy, and shorter wavelength means more energy.

answer.html: Yes, blue light (2.76 eV) can pump a red laser because its photons carry more than the 1.91 eV needed. No, infrared light (1.46 eV) cannot pump a yellow laser, because the photons have less than the 2.10 eV needed.

items.title: 49: Which characteristic of laser light is most important for each use: (a) welding steel, (b) sending data down an optical fiber using one color, (c) making a hologram, (d) shining a pointer spot on a far wall?

answer.html: (a) Welding: high power or intensity. (b) Fiber data: monochromatic (a single wavelength). (c) Hologram: coherent (waves in phase). (d) Far-wall pointer: directional (a narrow beam that spreads little).

items.title: 50 (Critical Thinking): Suppose an electron's cloud were squeezed from atomic size to a region of width 𝛥𝑥= 2.0 × 10−12 m. Use 𝑝≈ℎ/ (4𝜋𝛥𝑥) to estimate its kinetic energy and compare with the few eV it has in an atom.

body.html: The uncertainty principle: a smaller position uncertainty means a larger momentum.

answer.html: 𝐾𝐸≈2.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> eV (about 2.4 keV), a hundred or more times larger than the electron's few eV in an atom, so squeezing the cloud would take a large amount of energy.

check.html: The speed is 𝑝/ 𝑚≈2.9 × 10<sup>7</sup> m/s, about a tenth of 𝑐, so the non-relativistic formula is reasonable.

items.title: Science & Society, 3D Thinking: Use a model to describe how lasers are used to reshape the cornea of the eye in vision-correction surgery.

body.html: Open-ended research prompt. Here is a model response.

Visual model (flow): ultraviolet laser pulse, absorbed by corneal tissue, thin layer of tissue removed, cornea reshaped, light focuses properly on the retina. Labeled sketch parts: laser source, beam control, cornea, lens, retina. Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to break molecular bonds in the tissue (for example, 193 nm gives 1240 / 193 = 6.4 eV), so it removes material cleanly without much heating. The laser's narrow, intense beam lets the surgeon control exactly where it acts.

answer.html: Open-ended; a labeled diagram of laser, cornea, removed tissue and retina, as described above, summarizes the method.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (Electron cloud): Explain the meaning of the electron cloud.

answer.html: The electron cloud is the region around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding the electron. The electron does not have a fixed orbit; the density of the cloud shows how likely it is to be at each location.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 28 question: Compare the wavelengths of the incident and emitted photons in stimulated emission.

answer.html: They are the same. Both photons have energy 𝐸<sub>2</sub> −𝐸<sub>1</sub>, so they have the same wavelength (and frequency).

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (Stimulated emission): Compare the two photons emitted by stimulated emission.

answer.html: The two photons have the same energy, frequency and wavelength, they travel in the same direction and they are in phase (coherent).

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It? (Surveying): Which characteristics of laser light suit it to surveying and measuring large distances?

answer.html: The beam is narrow and highly directional (it spreads very little), intense, monochromatic and coherent, so it stays focused over long distances and can be detected after it bounces back.

items.title: Lesson 4, Investigate (Applying Practices, communicate technology information)

body.html: Sample: a fiber-optic network uses laser pulses on and off (wave interactions with matter: total internal reflection) to send data. A solar cell uses photons with enough energy to free electrons (photoelectric/photovoltaic effect) to produce current.

answer.html: Open-ended; the sample device descriptions above show the expected level of detail.

items.title: 47: Shortcomings of the Bohr model

answer.html: The model worked only for hydrogen and could not predict the spectrum of helium or any atom with more than one electron. It also gave no good reason why electromagnetic laws should work everywhere except inside the atom, and it pictured fixed orbits, whereas the quantum model gives only probabilities.

items.title: 48: Could green light pump a red laser? Could red light pump a green laser?

body.html: Pumping needs photons with energy at least as large as the atom's excitation energy, and shorter wavelength means more energy.
Green photons (about 2.3 eV) have more energy than red photons (about 1.9 eV).

answer.html: Yes, green light could pump a red laser because the photons have more than enough energy. Red light could not pump a green laser because red photons have less energy than the green transition requires.

items.title: 49: Four characteristics of laser light that make it useful

answer.html: Laser light is (1) coherent (waves in phase), (2) monochromatic (a single wavelength), (3) directional (a narrow beam with little spreading) and (4) powerful or intense. It can also be pulsed.

items.title: 50 (Critical Thinking): Why would shrinking the electron cloud to the size of the nucleus need a great deal of energy?

body.html: The uncertainty principle links position and momentum: a smaller position uncertainty means a larger momentum uncertainty.

If the electron is confined to the nucleus (𝛥𝑥∼10<sup>−</sup><sup>15</sup> m), its momentum uncertainty becomes huge, which means it must have a large momentum and hence a large kinetic energy. Estimate (beyond the text): 𝑝∼ℎ/ (4𝜋𝛥𝑥) = 6.63 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>34</sup> / (4𝜋× 1.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>15</sup>) ≈3.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>20</sup> kg · m/s, so 𝐾𝐸≈𝑝𝑐≈6.6 × 10<sup>7</sup> eV (tens of MeV), vastly more than the electron's few eV in an atom.

answer.html: Confining the electron to a region about the size of the nucleus makes its momentum uncertainty very large, so it would need a very large kinetic energy, and that energy would have to be supplied.

items.title: Science & Society, 3D Thinking: Use a model to describe how lasers detect tooth decay

body.html: Open-ended research prompt. Here is a model response.

Visual model (flow): infrared laser, reflected from tooth, infrared sensor; changes in the reflected light and heat map the location of decay under the enamel. Labeled sketch parts: laser source, tooth (enamel over dentin), cavity (reflects differently), sensor, display. Because decayed tissue absorbs and scatters light differently than healthy enamel, a change in the reflected signal marks a cavity.

answer.html: Open-ended; a labeled diagram of laser, tooth, cavity and sensor, as described above, summarizes the method.
